lessons.title: Notes & candidates
lessons.summary: The rules of sudoku and how notes help you think.
intro: Fill the grid so that every *row*, every *column* and every 3×3 *box* contains each digit 1–9 exactly once. That single rule is all there is — every technique in these lessons is just a clever consequence of it.

A *candidate* is a digit that could still go in an empty cell: it is not already in that cell's row, column or box. Writing candidates as small *notes* turns the puzzle into something you can reason about on paper.

Techniques do one of two things: they *place* a digit (shown in green) or they *remove* candidates (shown crossed out in red). Removing candidates is progress too — sooner or later a cell or a unit is left with just one option.

steps.text: A sudoku has 9 *rows*, 9 *columns* and 9 *boxes* (the 3×3 blocks with thick borders). Here row 1, column 2 and box 1 are shaded: each must end up with all digits 1–9, once each.
Cells are named by row and column: the highlighted cell is *r1c2* (row 1, column 2). Its row, column and box already contain 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9 (yellow).
So only 1, 2 and 5 can still go there. These are its *candidates*, written as small notes in the cell — each digit always in the same spot (1 top-left … 9 bottom-right).
The whole board with notes filled in looks like this. Every technique in these lessons reads these notes and finds a reason to *remove* a candidate (red, crossed out) or *place* a digit (green).
When a digit is placed, it removes that candidate from every cell in its row, column and box. Keeping notes tidy this way is what makes the patterns visible. Ready? Start with the full house.

lessons.title: Full House
lessons.summary: The last empty cell in a row, column or box.
intro: When a row, column or box has only *one empty cell* left, that cell must hold the one digit the unit is still missing.
It works because each unit needs all nine digits: eight are already there, so the ninth has exactly one place to go.
How to spot it: scan for units that are almost full. It is the easiest move in sudoku — always check for it first, especially late in a puzzle.

step.name: Full House
step.text: Full house: r5c5 is the last empty cell in row 5, so it must be 4.

steps.text: Look at *row 5*. Only one of its cells is still empty: r5c5.
Row 5 already holds 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9. The only digit missing is *4*.
So *r5c5 must be 4*. A full house is the easiest move there is — always check nearly full units first.

example.task: One row, column or box has a single empty cell. Tap the candidate that belongs there.

step.name: Full House
step.text: Full house: r3c3 is the last empty cell in row 3, so it must be 5.

steps.text: Look at *row 3*. Only one of its cells is still empty: r3c3.
Row 3 already holds 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 and 9. The only digit missing is *5*.
So *r3c3 must be 5*. A full house is the easiest move there is — always check nearly full units first.

practice.task: One row, column or box has a single empty cell. Tap the candidate that belongs there.

lessons.title: Naked Single
lessons.summary: A cell with only one candidate left.
intro: A *naked single* is a cell that has only one candidate left. Every other digit already appears in its row, its column or its box.
Since the cell must hold *some* digit and all others are ruled out, the remaining one is the answer.
How to spot it: with notes, look for a cell showing a single small digit. Without notes, pick a busy cell and count which digits its row, column and box already use.

step.name: Naked Single
step.text: Naked single: r1c4 has only one candidate left, so it must be 8.

steps.text: Look at *r1c4*. Its notes show just one candidate: 8.
Why? Its row 1, column 4 and box 2 together already contain 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 9 — every digit except 8.
A cell must hold some digit, and 8 is the only one left. So *r1c4 must be 8*.

example.task: Find a cell whose notes show only one candidate, and tap that candidate.

step.name: Naked Single
step.text: Naked single: r2c1 has only one candidate left, so it must be 1.

steps.text: Look at *r2c1*. Its notes show just one candidate: 1.
Why? Its row 2, column 1 and box 1 together already contain 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 — every digit except 1.
A cell must hold some digit, and 1 is the only one left. So *r2c1 must be 1*.

practice.task: Find a cell whose notes show only one candidate, and tap that candidate.

lessons.title: Hidden Single
lessons.summary: A digit with only one possible place in a unit.
intro: A *hidden single* looks at it from the digit's side: inside one row, column or box, a digit can go in *only one cell*. That cell may still show other notes — the single is "hidden" among them.
Every unit needs each digit exactly once. If all other cells of the unit are blocked for that digit (because they see the same digit elsewhere), the one remaining cell must take it.
How to spot it: pick a digit, follow where it already sits, and check each box, row and column for a lone free spot. This is the workhorse technique of easy and medium puzzles.

step.name: Hidden Single
step.text: Hidden single: in box 2, 8 can only go in r3c5.

steps.text: Focus on digit *8* in *box 2*. It has 5 empty cells — where can an 8 go?
The 8s already placed at r1c3 and r7c4 (yellow) rule out 8 along the shaded rows and columns. Every empty cell of box 2 is blocked — except one.
So 8 fits only in *r3c5* — even though its notes also show 5 and 6, the box needs its 8 and has no other place for it. *r3c5 = 8*.

example.task: Find a digit that fits in only one cell of some row, column or box, and tap that candidate.

step.name: Hidden Single
step.text: Hidden single: in box 2, 5 can only go in r3c4.

steps.text: Focus on digit *5* in *box 2*. It has 5 empty cells — where can a 5 go?
The 5s already placed at r1c7 and r2c2 (yellow) rule out 5 along the shaded rows. Every empty cell of box 2 is blocked — except one.
So 5 fits only in *r3c4* — even though its notes also show 1 and 7, the box needs its 5 and has no other place for it. *r3c4 = 5*.

practice.task: Find a digit that fits in only one cell of some row, column or box, and tap that candidate.

lessons.title: Pointing
lessons.summary: A digit locked to one line inside a box clears that line.
intro: Sometimes, inside a box, all candidates for a digit lie on *one row or one column*. The box must contain the digit somewhere, so it will end up on that line — the candidates "point" along it.
Because a row or column holds each digit only once, the digit cannot appear anywhere else on that line *outside the box*. Those candidates can be removed.
How to spot it: for each box, look at one digit's notes. If they form a short straight segment of two or three cells, follow the line out of the box and clear the digit.

step.name: Pointing
step.text: Pointing: in box 2, 4 is confined to column 5, so 4 can be removed from r5c5.

steps.text: Look at digit *4* in *box 2*. Its notes show 4 only in r1c5 and r3c5.
These cells all lie in *column 5*. Box 2 needs a 4, so whichever cell it is, that 4 will be in column 5.
Column 5 can hold only one 4, so the rest of the column outside box 2 cannot be 4: remove *4* from r5c5.

example.task: Find the pointing candidates and tap every candidate they remove, then press Check.

step.name: Pointing
step.text: Pointing: in box 8, 5 is confined to column 4, so 5 can be removed from r3c4.

steps.text: Look at digit *5* in *box 8*. Its notes show 5 only in r8c4 and r9c4.
These cells all lie in *column 4*. Box 8 needs a 5, so whichever cell it is, that 5 will be in column 4.
Column 4 can hold only one 5, so the rest of the column outside box 8 cannot be 5: remove *5* from r3c4.

practice.task: Find the pointing candidates and tap every candidate they remove, then press Check.

lessons.title: Claiming
lessons.summary: A digit locked to one box inside a line clears that box.
intro: *Claiming* (also called box/line reduction) is pointing turned around. In a row or column, all candidates for a digit lie inside *one box*.
The row needs that digit, and it can only get it inside this box — so the box's copy of the digit is used up by the row. Every other cell of the box loses that candidate.
How to spot it: look along a row or column for a digit whose notes are all in the same three-cell segment, then clear the digit from the rest of that box.

step.name: Claiming
step.text: Claiming: in row 7, 1 is confined to box 9, so 1 can be removed from r8c7.

steps.text: Look at digit *1* in *row 7*. Its notes show 1 only in r7c7 and r7c9.
All of them are inside *box 9*. Row 7 needs a 1, so it will take box 9's 1 — the box's 1 is on this row.
So no other cell of box 9 can be 1: remove *1* from r8c7.

example.task: Find where a line claims a digit for one box, and tap every candidate that is removed.

step.name: Claiming
step.text: Claiming: in row 7, 6 is confined to box 7, so 6 can be removed from r8c3, r9c1.

steps.text: Look at digit *6* in *row 7*. Its notes show 6 only in r7c1 and r7c3.
All of them are inside *box 7*. Row 7 needs a 6, so it will take box 7's 6 — the box's 6 is on this row.
So no other cell of box 7 can be 6: remove *6* from r8c3 and r9c1.

practice.task: Find where a line claims a digit for one box, and tap every candidate that is removed.

lessons.title: Naked Pair
lessons.summary: Two cells with the same two candidates.
intro: A *naked pair* is two cells in one unit that both contain exactly the same *two candidates*, for example {3,8} and {3,8}.
Those two cells must take those two digits between them — one gets 3, the other 8, we don't yet know which. Either way, both digits are used up, so no other cell in that unit can be 3 or 8.
How to spot it: look for twin two-digit notes in the same row, column or box. If the pair also shares a box, it clears both units.

step.name: Naked Pair
step.text: Naked pair: in row 6, cells r6c2, r6c9 can only hold 1 and 3, so these digits can be removed from the other cells of the row (r6c7, r6c8).

steps.text: Look at *row 6* and the cells with only two candidates.
These two cells contain only the digits *1 and 3*: r6c2 {1,3}, r6c9 {1,3}.

Two cells need two different digits, and only these two are available to them. So the cells will take exactly 1 and 3 between them — we don't know the order yet, but the digits are used up. That's a naked pair.
So 1 and 3 can be removed from every other cell of the row: remove *1* from r6c7 and *3* from r6c8.

example.task: Find the naked pair and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: Naked Pair
step.text: Naked pair: in row 8, cells r8c6, r8c9 can only hold 6 and 8, so these digits can be removed from the other cells of the row (r8c5).

steps.text: Look at *row 8* and the cells with only two candidates.
These two cells contain only the digits *6 and 8*: r8c6 {6,8}, r8c9 {6,8}.

Two cells need two different digits, and only these two are available to them. So the cells will take exactly 6 and 8 between them — we don't know the order yet, but the digits are used up. That's a naked pair.
So 6 and 8 can be removed from every other cell of the row: remove *6* from r8c5.

practice.task: Find the naked pair and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: Hidden Pair
lessons.summary: Two digits that fit in only the same two cells.
intro: A *hidden pair* is two digits that, within one unit, can only go in the *same two cells*. The cells may show other notes too — the pair is hidden among them.
Those two cells must hold those two digits (each digit needs a home, and there are only two homes). So any *other* candidate in the two cells is impossible and can be removed.
How to spot it: in a unit, look for two digits that each appear exactly twice, in the same two cells. After the clean-up, the cells become a naked pair.

step.name: Hidden Pair
step.text: Hidden pair: in row 6, 3 and 8 can only go in r6c1, r6c5, so all other candidates can be removed from these cells.

steps.text: Look at digits *3 and 8* in *row 6*. Where can each of them go?
3 in r6c1 and r6c5; 8 in r6c1 and r6c5. Together they fit only in the same two cells: r6c1 and r6c5.
Two digits need two homes and have exactly two, so these cells are reserved for 3 and 8 — a hidden pair. Any other candidate in them is impossible.
Remove the other candidates: *1* from r6c5. Now the two cells form a naked pair.

example.task: Find the hidden pair and tap every other candidate in its two cells, then press Check.

step.name: Hidden Pair
step.text: Hidden pair: in box 9, 2 and 4 can only go in r7c9, r8c8, so all other candidates can be removed from these cells.

steps.text: Look at digits *2 and 4* in *box 9*. Where can each of them go?
2 in r7c9 and r8c8; 4 in r7c9 and r8c8. Together they fit only in the same two cells: r7c9 and r8c8.
Two digits need two homes and have exactly two, so these cells are reserved for 2 and 4 — a hidden pair. Any other candidate in them is impossible.
Remove the other candidates: *3* from r7c9 and *8* from r8c8. Now the two cells form a naked pair.

practice.task: Find the hidden pair and tap every other candidate in its two cells, then press Check.

lessons.title: Naked Triple
lessons.summary: Three cells that use only three digits.
intro: A *naked triple* is three cells in one unit whose candidates, together, contain only *three digits*. Not every cell needs all three: {1,4}, {4,7}, {1,7} is a perfect triple.
Three cells need three different digits, and only three are available to them — so these three digits are used up by these cells. Remove them from every other cell of the unit.
How to spot it: look for cells with two or three candidates drawn from the same small set of digits. It is the naked pair idea with one more cell.

step.name: Naked Triple
step.text: Naked triple: in column 6, cells r3c6, r4c6, r7c6 can only hold 3, 4 and 7, so these digits can be removed from the other cells of the column (r1c6).

steps.text: Look at *column 6* and the cells with two or three candidates.
These three cells contain only the digits *3, 4 and 7*: r3c6 {3,4}, r4c6 {3,7}, r7c6 {4,7}.

Three cells need three different digits, and only these three are available to them. So the cells will take exactly 3, 4 and 7 between them — we don't know the order yet, but the digits are used up. That's a naked triple.
So 3, 4 and 7 can be removed from every other cell of the column: remove *4* from r1c6.

example.task: Find the naked triple and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: Naked Triple
step.text: Naked triple: in column 7, cells r2c7, r3c7, r7c7 can only hold 2, 5 and 7, so these digits can be removed from the other cells of the column (r4c7, r8c7).

steps.text: Look at *column 7* and the cells with two or three candidates.
These three cells contain only the digits *2, 5 and 7*: r2c7 {2,5}, r3c7 {5,7}, r7c7 {2,7}.

Three cells need three different digits, and only these three are available to them. So the cells will take exactly 2, 5 and 7 between them — we don't know the order yet, but the digits are used up. That's a naked triple.
So 2, 5 and 7 can be removed from every other cell of the column: remove *7* from r4c7 and *2* from r8c7.

practice.task: Find the naked triple and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: Hidden Triple
lessons.summary: Three digits squeezed into the same three cells.
intro: A *hidden triple* is three digits that, within one unit, can only go in the *same three cells* (each digit in two or three of them).
Three digits need three homes and have exactly three — so those cells are reserved for them. Every other candidate in those three cells can be removed.
How to spot it: count, per digit, how many cells of the unit can take it. Digits with only two or three spots are the ones to test. Hidden triples are hard to see; notes make them visible.

step.name: Hidden Triple
step.text: Hidden triple: in row 7, 3, 7 and 9 can only go in r7c1, r7c5, r7c9, so all other candidates can be removed from these cells.

steps.text: Look at digits *3, 7 and 9* in *row 7*. Where can each of them go?
3 in r7c1 and r7c9; 7 in r7c1 and r7c5; 9 in r7c5 and r7c9. Together they fit only in the same three cells: r7c1, r7c5 and r7c9.
Three digits need three homes and have exactly three, so these cells are reserved for 3, 7 and 9 — a hidden triple. Any other candidate in them is impossible.
Remove the other candidates: *8* from r7c1. Now the three cells form a naked triple.

example.task: Find the hidden triple and tap every other candidate in its three cells, then press Check.

step.name: Hidden Triple
step.text: Hidden triple: in box 1, 1, 3 and 8 can only go in r1c1, r1c2, r3c2, so all other candidates can be removed from these cells.

steps.text: Look at digits *1, 3 and 8* in *box 1*. Where can each of them go?
1 in r1c1, r1c2 and r3c2; 3 in r1c1 and r1c2; 8 in r1c2 and r3c2. Together they fit only in the same three cells: r1c1, r1c2 and r3c2.
Three digits need three homes and have exactly three, so these cells are reserved for 1, 3 and 8 — a hidden triple. Any other candidate in them is impossible.
Remove the other candidates: *7* from r1c1. Now the three cells form a naked triple.

practice.task: Find the hidden triple and tap every other candidate in its three cells, then press Check.

lessons.title: Naked Quad
lessons.summary: Four cells that use only four digits.
intro: A *naked quad* is four cells in one unit whose candidates together contain only *four digits*.
The logic is the same as for pairs and triples: four cells, four digits, so the digits are used up by these cells and can be removed from the rest of the unit.

How to spot it: it usually shows up in a unit with many empty cells. If a unit has N empty cells and a naked quad, the other N−4 cells form a hidden subset — sometimes that is the easier way to see it.

step.name: Naked Quad
step.text: Naked quad: in column 1, cells r2c1, r7c1, r8c1, r9c1 can only hold 1, 2, 5 and 7, so these digits can be removed from the other cells of the column (r4c1, r5c1).

steps.text: Look at *column 1* and the cells with two to four candidates.
These four cells contain only the digits *1, 2, 5 and 7*: r2c1 {5,7}, r7c1 {1,2}, r8c1 {2,5,7}, r9c1 {1,2,5}.

Four cells need four different digits, and only these four are available to them. So the cells will take exactly 1, 2, 5 and 7 between them — we don't know the order yet, but the digits are used up. That's a naked quad.
So 1, 2, 5 and 7 can be removed from every other cell of the column: remove *7* from r4c1 and r5c1.

example.task: Find the naked quad and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: Naked Quad
step.text: Naked quad: in row 5, cells r5c4, r5c7, r5c8, r5c9 can only hold 2, 4, 5 and 8, so these digits can be removed from the other cells of the row (r5c6).

steps.text: Look at *row 5* and the cells with two to four candidates.
These four cells contain only the digits *2, 4, 5 and 8*: r5c4 {5,8}, r5c7 {2,5,8}, r5c8 {2,4,5}, r5c9 {4,8}.

Four cells need four different digits, and only these four are available to them. So the cells will take exactly 2, 4, 5 and 8 between them — we don't know the order yet, but the digits are used up. That's a naked quad.
So 2, 4, 5 and 8 can be removed from every other cell of the row: remove *5* and *8* from r5c6.

practice.task: Find the naked quad and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: Hidden Quad
lessons.summary: Four digits squeezed into the same four cells.
intro: A *hidden quad* is four digits that, within one unit, can only go in the *same four cells*.
Those four cells are therefore reserved for those four digits, and every other candidate in them can go.

How to spot it: it is rare and almost always appears in a unit with many empty cells. The trick is to look for digits with few positions in the unit and check whether four of them share the same cells.

step.name: Hidden Quad
step.text: Hidden quad: in row 5, 1, 3, 8 and 9 can only go in r5c2, r5c3, r5c7, r5c9, so all other candidates can be removed from these cells.

steps.text: Look at digits *1, 3, 8 and 9* in *row 5*. Where can each of them go?
1 in r5c2 and r5c9; 3 in r5c2 and r5c7; 8 in r5c3 and r5c7; 9 in r5c3 and r5c9. Together they fit only in the same four cells: r5c2, r5c3, r5c7 and r5c9.
Four digits need four homes and have exactly four, so these cells are reserved for 1, 3, 8 and 9 — a hidden quad. Any other candidate in them is impossible.
Remove the other candidates: *2* from r5c7. Now the four cells form a naked quad.

example.task: Find the hidden quad and tap every other candidate in its four cells, then press Check.

step.name: Hidden Quad
step.text: Hidden quad: in row 8, 2, 4, 7 and 9 can only go in r8c1, r8c3, r8c4, r8c9, so all other candidates can be removed from these cells.

steps.text: Look at digits *2, 4, 7 and 9* in *row 8*. Where can each of them go?
2 in r8c4 and r8c9; 4 in r8c1 and r8c3; 7 in r8c1, r8c3 and r8c4; 9 in r8c3 and r8c9. Together they fit only in the same four cells: r8c1, r8c3, r8c4 and r8c9.
Four digits need four homes and have exactly four, so these cells are reserved for 2, 4, 7 and 9 — a hidden quad. Any other candidate in them is impossible.
Remove the other candidates: *6* from r8c3. Now the four cells form a naked quad.

practice.task: Find the hidden quad and tap every other candidate in its four cells, then press Check.

lessons.title: X-Wing
lessons.summary: Two rows, two columns, one digit: a rectangle.
intro: Pick one digit. If in *two rows* that digit can only go in the *same two columns*, the four spots form the corners of a rectangle: an *X-Wing*.

Each of the two rows needs the digit once, and both must use those two columns. So one copy goes in each column — they fill the two columns between them. No other cell in those two columns can hold the digit.
The same works with rows and columns swapped. How to spot it: for one digit, look for rows (or columns) where it has exactly two spots, and check whether two of them line up.

step.name: X-Wing
step.text: X-Wing on 4 in rows 6 and 8 (columns 3 and 5): 4 can be removed from r7c5.

steps.text: Look only at digit *4* in rows 6 and 8. In each of these rows, 4 has just two places: row 6: r6c3 and r6c5; row 8: r8c3 and r8c5.
All of these candidates lie in only two columns: *columns 3 and 5*. The four cells are the corners of a rectangle.
Each of the two rows needs one 4, and each must take it in one of these two columns. Two 4s in two columns, at most one per column: they fill the columns completely. That's an X-Wing.
So no other cell in columns 3 and 5 can be 4: remove *4* from r7c5.

example.task: Find the X-Wing and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: X-Wing
step.text: X-Wing on 3 in rows 2 and 6 (columns 3 and 9): 3 can be removed from r5c9.

steps.text: Look only at digit *3* in rows 2 and 6. In each of these rows, 3 has just two places: row 2: r2c3 and r2c9; row 6: r6c3 and r6c9.
All of these candidates lie in only two columns: *columns 3 and 9*. The four cells are the corners of a rectangle.
Each of the two rows needs one 3, and each must take it in one of these two columns. Two 3s in two columns, at most one per column: they fill the columns completely. That's an X-Wing.
So no other cell in columns 3 and 9 can be 3: remove *3* from r5c9.

practice.task: Find the X-Wing and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: Skyscraper
lessons.summary: Two strong links on one digit with a shared base.
intro: A *skyscraper* uses two rows (or two columns) where a digit has *exactly two places*. One end of each lines up in the same column — the base — while the other two ends (the tops) do not.
The two base cells see each other, so at most one of them holds the digit. In the row whose base is empty, the digit must sit at the top. So *at least one top* holds the digit.
Any cell that sees *both tops* can therefore not hold the digit. Think of it as an X-Wing with one leg bent.

step.name: Skyscraper
step.text: Skyscraper on 3: in row 1 and row 7, 3 has only two places each, and r1c8 and r7c8 share a column. So r1c2 or r7c3 must be 3, and 3 can be removed from r2c3.

steps.text: Look only at digit *3*. In row 1 it has only two places (r1c2 and r1c8), and in row 7 too (r7c3 and r7c8). Each pair is a *strong link*: one of the two must be 3.
r1c8 and r7c8 share a column — the base of the skyscraper. They see each other, so at most one of them is 3.
If r1c8 is not 3, then r1c2 is. If r7c8 is not 3, then r7c3 is. One of the base cells is not 3, so *r1c2 or r7c3 is 3*.
A cell that sees both tops can't be 3: remove *3* from r2c3.

example.task: Find the skyscraper and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: Skyscraper
step.text: Skyscraper on 9: in row 4 and row 9, 9 has only two places each, and r4c7 and r9c7 share a column. So r4c2 or r9c1 must be 9, and 9 can be removed from r6c1.

steps.text: Look only at digit *9*. In row 4 it has only two places (r4c2 and r4c7), and in row 9 too (r9c1 and r9c7). Each pair is a *strong link*: one of the two must be 9.
r4c7 and r9c7 share a column — the base of the skyscraper. They see each other, so at most one of them is 9.
If r4c7 is not 9, then r4c2 is. If r9c7 is not 9, then r9c1 is. One of the base cells is not 9, so *r4c2 or r9c1 is 9*.
A cell that sees both tops can't be 9: remove *9* from r6c1.

practice.task: Find the skyscraper and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: 2-String Kite
lessons.summary: A row and a column joined through a box.
intro: A *2-String Kite* combines a row and a column where one digit has *exactly two places* each. One end of the row's pair and one end of the column's pair sit in the *same box*.

Those two box cells see each other, so at most one holds the digit. If the row's box cell is empty, the row's other end has the digit; likewise for the column. So *at least one of the two far ends* holds the digit.
The cell at the crossing of the far ends' row and column sees both of them, so it cannot hold the digit.

step.name: 2-String Kite
step.text: 2-String Kite on 9: 9 has only two places in row 7 and in column 4; r7c6 and r8c4 share box 8, so r7c8 or r3c4 must be 9. r3c8 sees both, so 9 can be removed from it.

steps.text: Look only at digit *9*. In row 7 it has only two places (r7c6 and r7c8), and in column 4 only two (r3c4 and r8c4). These are two strings (strong links).
r7c6 and r8c4 are in the same box (box 8), so at most one of them is 9.
If r7c6 is not 9, r7c8 is; if r8c4 is not 9, r3c4 is. So *r7c8 or r3c4 is 9*.
r3c8 sits in r7c8's column and r3c4's row, so it sees both ends: remove *9* from r3c8.

example.task: Find the 2-String Kite and tap the candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: 2-String Kite
step.text: 2-String Kite on 8: 8 has only two places in row 2 and in column 1; r2c3 and r1c1 share box 1, so r2c5 or r4c1 must be 8. r4c5 sees both, so 8 can be removed from it.

steps.text: Look only at digit *8*. In row 2 it has only two places (r2c3 and r2c5), and in column 1 only two (r1c1 and r4c1). These are two strings (strong links).
r2c3 and r1c1 are in the same box (box 1), so at most one of them is 8.
If r2c3 is not 8, r2c5 is; if r1c1 is not 8, r4c1 is. So *r2c5 or r4c1 is 8*.
r4c5 sits in r2c5's column and r4c1's row, so it sees both ends: remove *8* from r4c5.

lessons.title: Empty Rectangle
lessons.summary: A box whose candidates form a cross.
intro: Inside one box, look at one digit. If all its candidates lie on *one row plus one column* of the box (a cross, leaving an "empty rectangle" of cells without the digit), the box's copy must be on that row or on that column.

Now find a line outside the box where the digit has *exactly two places*, one of them on the cross's row (or column). If a target cell would make the box's cross impossible from both sides, it cannot hold the digit.
It sounds tricky, but on the board it is a small picture: a box cross, one strong link, and one cell that would break both arms.

step.name: Empty Rectangle
step.text: Empty rectangle on 3: in box 5, 3 lies only in row 6 or column 5. 3 has only two places in column 7 (r6c7, r8c7). If r8c5 were 3, r6c7 would be 3 too and box 5 would have no place for 3. So 3 can be removed from r8c5.

steps.text: Look only at digit *3* in *box 5*: its candidates are r4c5, r5c5, r6c5 and r6c6. They all lie in row 6 or column 5 — a cross. The other cells of the box (the "empty rectangle") have no 3.
So the 3 of box 5 is in row 6 or in column 5. Now look at column 7: 3 has only two places there, r6c7 and r8c7 — a strong link, and r6c7 is on the cross's row 6.
Suppose r8c5 were 3. It shares a row with r8c7, so r8c7 is not 3 and r6c7 must be. r6c7 blocks row 6 of the box, and r8c5 blocks column 5 — box 5 would have no place left for 3.
That's impossible, so remove *3* from r8c5.

example.task: Find the empty rectangle and tap the candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: Empty Rectangle
step.text: Empty rectangle on 5: in box 8, 5 lies only in row 7 or column 4. 5 has only two places in row 2 (r2c4, r2c3). If r7c3 were 5, r2c4 would be 5 too and box 8 would have no place for 5. So 5 can be removed from r7c3.

steps.text: Look only at digit *5* in *box 8*: its candidates are r7c5 and r8c4. They all lie in row 7 or column 4 — a cross. The other cells of the box (the "empty rectangle") have no 5.
So the 5 of box 8 is in row 7 or in column 4. Now look at row 2: 5 has only two places there, r2c4 and r2c3 — a strong link, and r2c4 is on the cross's column 4.
Suppose r7c3 were 5. It shares a column with r2c3, so r2c3 is not 5 and r2c4 must be. r2c4 blocks column 4 of the box, and r7c3 blocks row 7 — box 8 would have no place left for 5.
That's impossible, so remove *5* from r7c3.

practice.task: Find the empty rectangle and tap the candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: XY-Wing
lessons.summary: A pivot with two candidates and two pincers.
intro: An *XY-Wing* uses three cells with exactly two candidates each: a *pivot* {X,Y} and two *pincers* it can see, {X,Z} and {Y,Z}.
If the pivot is X, the first pincer cannot be X, so it is Z. If the pivot is Y, the second pincer becomes Z. Either way, *one of the pincers is Z*.
So any cell that sees *both pincers* cannot be Z. How to spot it: look at two-candidate cells, and search for a pivot whose two digits each continue into a pincer with a shared third digit.

step.name: XY-Wing
step.text: XY-Wing: pivot r7c8 {68} with pincers r6c8 {62} and r7c1 {82}. Whatever the pivot is, one pincer must be 2, so 2 can be removed from r6c1.

steps.text: Look at *r7c8*: it has exactly two candidates, *6* and *8*. This is the pivot.
The pivot sees two pincers with two candidates each: r6c8 {2,6} shares 6 with it, and r7c1 {2,8} shares 8. Both pincers also contain *2*.
If r7c8 is 6, then r6c8 can't be 6, so it is 2. If r7c8 is 8, then r7c1 is 2. Either way, *one of the pincers is 2*.
Any cell that sees both pincers can't be 2: remove *2* from r6c1.

example.task: Find the XY-Wing and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: XY-Wing
step.text: XY-Wing: pivot r2c5 {26} with pincers r2c8 {28} and r7c5 {68}. Whatever the pivot is, one pincer must be 8, so 8 can be removed from r7c8.

steps.text: Look at *r2c5*: it has exactly two candidates, *2* and *6*. This is the pivot.
The pivot sees two pincers with two candidates each: r2c8 {2,8} shares 2 with it, and r7c5 {6,8} shares 6. Both pincers also contain *8*.
If r2c5 is 2, then r2c8 can't be 2, so it is 8. If r2c5 is 6, then r7c5 is 8. Either way, *one of the pincers is 8*.
Any cell that sees both pincers can't be 8: remove *8* from r7c8.

practice.task: Find the XY-Wing and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: W-Wing
lessons.summary: Two identical pairs connected by a strong link.
intro: A *W-Wing* starts with two cells that hold the *same two candidates* {X,Y} but do not see each other.

Now find a unit where X has *only two places*, one seeing each of the two cells. If both cells were X, neither of those places could be X — but the unit needs its X. So *at least one of the two cells is Y*.
Any cell that sees both {X,Y} cells can therefore not be Y.

step.name: W-Wing
step.text: W-Wing: r1c7 and r7c5 both hold {24}, and 2 in column 2 must be in r1c2 or r7c2. They cannot both be 2, so one of them is 4: 4 can be removed from r7c7.

steps.text: r1c7 and r7c5 both hold exactly *{2,4}*, and they don't see each other.
In *column 2*, 2 has only two places: r1c2 and r7c2 (a strong link). r1c2 sees r1c7, and r7c2 sees r7c5.
If both r1c7 and r7c5 were 2, neither r1c2 nor r7c2 could be 2 — and column 2 would have no 2. So *at least one of them is 4*.
Any cell that sees both r1c7 and r7c5 can't be 4: remove *4* from r7c7.

example.task: Find the W-Wing and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: W-Wing
step.text: W-Wing: r4c6 and r8c1 both hold {51}, and 5 in column 8 must be in r4c8 or r8c8. They cannot both be 5, so one of them is 1: 1 can be removed from r8c6.

steps.text: r4c6 and r8c1 both hold exactly *{1,5}*, and they don't see each other.
In *column 8*, 5 has only two places: r4c8 and r8c8 (a strong link). r4c8 sees r4c6, and r8c8 sees r8c1.
If both r4c6 and r8c1 were 5, neither r4c8 nor r8c8 could be 5 — and column 8 would have no 5. So *at least one of them is 1*.
Any cell that sees both r4c6 and r8c1 can't be 1: remove *1* from r8c6.

practice.task: Find the W-Wing and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: Simple Coloring
lessons.summary: Follow one digit's strong links in two colours.
intro: Take one digit and find its *strong links*: units where it has exactly two places, so exactly one of them is true. Connected strong links form a chain of cells.
Colour the chain alternately A, B, A, B… Within the chain, either all A cells hold the digit or all B cells do — one colour is true, the other false.
Two rules follow. *Trap*: a cell that sees one A cell and one B cell cannot hold the digit. *Wrap*: if two cells of the same colour see each other, that colour is false everywhere.

step.name: Simple Coloring
step.text: Simple coloring on 6 (color trap): following the strong links for 6, one of the two colors must be true. r5c9 sees both colors, so 6 can be removed from r5c9.

steps.text: Look only at digit *6* and its *strong links* — units where 6 has exactly two places. Connected, they form a chain through 6 cells.
Colour the chain alternately: teal and orange. Along a strong link exactly one end is 6, so either *every teal* cell is 6, or *every orange* cell is.
r5c9 sees a teal cell *and* an orange cell. Whichever colour is true, it would see a 6.
So remove *6* from r5c9.

example.task: Colour the strong links of one digit and tap every candidate that is removed, then press Check.

step.name: Simple Coloring
step.text: Simple coloring on 8 (color trap): following the strong links for 8, one of the two colors must be true. r1c1, r1c8 see both colors, so 8 can be removed from r1c1, r1c8.

steps.text: Look only at digit *8* and its *strong links* — units where 8 has exactly two places. Connected, they form a chain through 6 cells.
Colour the chain alternately: teal and orange. Along a strong link exactly one end is 8, so either *every teal* cell is 8, or *every orange* cell is.
r1c1 and r1c8 see a teal cell *and* an orange cell. Whichever colour is true, they would see a 8.
So remove *8* from r1c1 and r1c8.

practice.task: Colour the strong links of one digit and tap every candidate that is removed, then press Check.

lessons.title: Swordfish
lessons.summary: An X-Wing with three rows and three columns.
intro: A *swordfish* is the X-Wing idea with three lines. In *three rows*, one digit fits only within the *same three columns* (each row having two or three spots).
The three rows each need the digit once, and all of them must use those three columns — so the three copies fill the three columns, one per column. Every other candidate in those columns can go.
How to spot it: for one digit, list the rows where it has two or three spots and look for three of them that together touch only three columns. Rows and columns can be swapped.

step.name: Swordfish
step.text: Swordfish on 5 in rows 1, 3 and 8 (columns 3, 4 and 8): 5 can be removed from r5c4, r9c8.

steps.text: Look only at digit *5* in rows 1, 3 and 8. In each of these rows, 5 has just two or three places: row 1: r1c3 and r1c8; row 3: r3c3 and r3c4; row 8: r8c4 and r8c8.
All of these candidates lie in only three columns: *columns 3, 4 and 8*.
Each of the three rows needs one 5, and each must take it in one of these three columns. Three 5s in three columns, at most one per column: they fill the columns completely. That's a Swordfish.
So no other cell in columns 3, 4 and 8 can be 5: remove *5* from r5c4 and r9c8.

example.task: Find the swordfish and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: Swordfish
step.text: Swordfish on 8 in rows 2, 4 and 8 (columns 5, 8 and 9): 8 can be removed from r6c5, r5c8, r3c9.

steps.text: Look only at digit *8* in rows 2, 4 and 8. In each of these rows, 8 has just two or three places: row 2: r2c5 and r2c9; row 4: r4c5 and r4c8; row 8: r8c8 and r8c9.
All of these candidates lie in only three columns: *columns 5, 8 and 9*.
Each of the three rows needs one 8, and each must take it in one of these three columns. Three 8s in three columns, at most one per column: they fill the columns completely. That's a Swordfish.
So no other cell in columns 5, 8 and 9 can be 8: remove *8* from r3c9, r5c8 and r6c5.

practice.task: Find the swordfish and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: Jellyfish
lessons.summary: The fish pattern with four rows and four columns.
intro: A *jellyfish* is the four-line fish: in *four rows*, one digit fits only within the *same four columns*.
Four rows, four copies of the digit, all confined to four columns — so they fill those columns, one each. The digit can be removed from every other cell of those four columns.
Jellyfish are rare. If you already know the X-Wing and swordfish, you know everything: base lines, cover lines, and eliminations in the cover lines outside the base.

step.name: Jellyfish
step.text: Jellyfish on 1 in rows 3, 5, 6 and 7 (columns 1, 2, 4 and 7): 1 can be removed from r4c2, r2c4, r2c7.

steps.text: Look only at digit *1* in rows 3, 5, 6 and 7. In each of these rows, 1 has just two to four places: row 3: r3c4 and r3c7; row 5: r5c2 and r5c7; row 6: r6c1 and r6c4; row 7: r7c1 and r7c2.
All of these candidates lie in only four columns: *columns 1, 2, 4 and 7*.
Each of the four rows needs one 1, and each must take it in one of these four columns. Four 1s in four columns, at most one per column: they fill the columns completely. That's a Jellyfish.
So no other cell in columns 1, 2, 4 and 7 can be 1: remove *1* from r2c4, r2c7 and r4c2.

example.task: Find the jellyfish and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: Jellyfish
step.text: Jellyfish on 5 in rows 4, 6, 8 and 9 (columns 1, 3, 5 and 9): 5 can be removed from r2c1, r5c1, r7c1, r2c3, r3c3, r7c9.

steps.text: Look only at digit *5* in rows 4, 6, 8 and 9. In each of these rows, 5 has just two to four places: row 4: r4c3 and r4c9; row 6: r6c1, r6c3 and r6c5; row 8: r8c5 and r8c9; row 9: r9c1, r9c3 and r9c9.
All of these candidates lie in only four columns: *columns 1, 3, 5 and 9*.
Each of the four rows needs one 5, and each must take it in one of these four columns. Four 5s in four columns, at most one per column: they fill the columns completely. That's a Jellyfish.
So no other cell in columns 1, 3, 5 and 9 can be 5: remove *5* from r2c1, r2c3, r3c3, r5c1, r7c1 and r7c9.

practice.task: Find the jellyfish and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: Finned X-Wing
lessons.summary: An X-Wing with an extra candidate in one corner box.
intro: A *finned X-Wing* is an X-Wing that is almost perfect: one row has one or two extra candidates, the *fin*, sitting in the same box as one of the X-Wing corners.
Either the fin holds the digit, or it does not — and then the X-Wing is real. In the first case the fin removes the digit from its box; in the second the X-Wing removes it from its columns.
Only cells hit by *both* cases are safe to clear: cells in the X-Wing's columns that are also in the fin's box.

step.name: Finned X-Wing
step.text: Finned X-Wing on 6 in rows 2 and 6 (columns 5 and 9, fin r2c6): either the X-Wing holds or a fin is 6; both remove 6 from r1c5.

steps.text: Look only at digit *6* in rows 2 and 6. Its candidates there are r2c5, r2c6, r2c9, r6c5 and r6c9.
Ignore r2c6 for a moment: the rest lie in only two columns, columns 5 and 9 — that would be an X-Wing.
The extra candidate r2c6 is the *fin*, all in box 2. Either a fin is 6, or the X-Wing is real — one of the two must hold.
If the X-Wing is real, 6 leaves the rest of its columns. If a fin is 6, 6 leaves box 2. Cells in both — a cover column *and* box 2 — lose 6 either way: remove *6* from r1c5.

example.task: Find the finned X-Wing and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: Finned X-Wing
step.text: Finned X-Wing on 8 in rows 3 and 9 (columns 2 and 8, fin r3c7): either the X-Wing holds or a fin is 8; both remove 8 from r1c8.

steps.text: Look only at digit *8* in rows 3 and 9. Its candidates there are r3c2, r3c7, r3c8, r9c2 and r9c8.
Ignore r3c7 for a moment: the rest lie in only two columns, columns 2 and 8 — that would be an X-Wing.
The extra candidate r3c7 is the *fin*, all in box 3. Either a fin is 8, or the X-Wing is real — one of the two must hold.
If the X-Wing is real, 8 leaves the rest of its columns. If a fin is 8, 8 leaves box 3. Cells in both — a cover column *and* box 3 — lose 8 either way: remove *8* from r1c8.

practice.task: Find the finned X-Wing and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: Finned Swordfish
lessons.summary: A swordfish with a fin.
intro: A *finned swordfish* is a swordfish with one or two extra candidates (the fin) in a single box.
Either one of the fin cells holds the digit, or the swordfish is real. Cells that would lose the digit in both cases — in a cover column and in the fin's box — can be cleared.
The pattern is identical to the finned X-Wing, just with three lines instead of two.

step.name: Finned Swordfish
step.text: Finned Swordfish on 3 in rows 1, 6 and 7 (columns 1, 4 and 6, fin r6c5): either the Swordfish holds or a fin is 3; both remove 3 from r5c4.

steps.text: Look only at digit *3* in rows 1, 6 and 7. Its candidates there are r1c1, r1c6, r6c1, r6c4, r6c5, r7c4 and r7c6.
Ignore r6c5 for a moment: the rest lie in only three columns, columns 1, 4 and 6 — that would be a Swordfish.
The extra candidate r6c5 is the *fin*, all in box 5. Either a fin is 3, or the Swordfish is real — one of the two must hold.
If the Swordfish is real, 3 leaves the rest of its columns. If a fin is 3, 3 leaves box 5. Cells in both — a cover column *and* box 5 — lose 3 either way: remove *3* from r5c4.

example.task: Find the finned swordfish and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: Finned Swordfish
step.text: Finned Swordfish on 6 in columns 2, 5 and 9 (rows 1, 3 and 7, fin r8c9): either the Swordfish holds or a fin is 6; both remove 6 from r7c7.

steps.text: Look only at digit *6* in columns 2, 5 and 9. Its candidates there are r1c2, r1c9, r3c2, r3c5, r7c5, r7c9 and r8c9.
Ignore r8c9 for a moment: the rest lie in only three rows, rows 1, 3 and 7 — that would be a Swordfish.
The extra candidate r8c9 is the *fin*, all in box 9. Either a fin is 6, or the Swordfish is real — one of the two must hold.
If the Swordfish is real, 6 leaves the rest of its rows. If a fin is 6, 6 leaves box 9. Cells in both — a cover row *and* box 9 — lose 6 either way: remove *6* from r7c7.

practice.task: Find the finned swordfish and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: XYZ-Wing
lessons.summary: An XY-Wing whose pivot also holds Z.
intro: An *XYZ-Wing* is like an XY-Wing, but the *pivot has three candidates* {X,Y,Z}, and the pincers are {X,Z} and {Y,Z}.
If the pivot is X, the {X,Z} pincer becomes Z; if it is Y, the {Y,Z} pincer becomes Z; and if it is Z itself, fine. In every case *one of the three cells is Z*.
So Z can be removed from any cell that sees *all three* — which means it must share the pivot's box and a line with a pincer.

step.name: XYZ-Wing
step.text: XYZ-Wing: pivot r4c1 {349} with pincers r4c2 {39} and r8c1 {49}. One of the three must be 9, so 9 can be removed from r5c1.

steps.text: The pivot *r4c1* has three candidates: {3,4,9}.
It sees two pincers: r4c2 {3,9} and r8c1 {4,9}. All three cells contain *9*.
If the pivot is 3, r4c2 must be 9. If it is 4, r8c1 must be 9. If it is 9, the pivot itself is. So *one of the three cells is 9*.
A cell that sees all three can't be 9: remove *9* from r5c1.

example.task: Find the XYZ-Wing and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: XYZ-Wing
step.text: XYZ-Wing: pivot r4c6 {156} with pincers r4c4 {16} and r9c6 {15}. One of the three must be 1, so 1 can be removed from r6c6.

steps.text: The pivot *r4c6* has three candidates: {1,5,6}.
It sees two pincers: r4c4 {1,6} and r9c6 {1,5}. All three cells contain *1*.
If the pivot is 6, r4c4 must be 1. If it is 5, r9c6 must be 1. If it is 1, the pivot itself is. So *one of the three cells is 1*.
A cell that sees all three can't be 1: remove *1* from r6c6.

practice.task: Find the XYZ-Wing and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle
lessons.summary: Avoid a rectangle that would allow two solutions.
intro: A proper sudoku has *exactly one solution*. Four cells forming a rectangle across *two boxes* that could all be just {A,B} are a "deadly pattern": you could swap A and B and get a second solution.

So the puzzle must prevent that. If three corners hold only {A,B}, the fourth corner cannot be A or B (*type 1*). If two corners have one shared extra digit, one of them must take it (*type 2*). If a digit is locked into the two extra corners, the other rectangle digit goes (*type 4*).
Use this only with puzzles that have a unique solution — which all puzzles in this app do.

step.name: Unique Rectangle
step.text: Unique rectangle r7c2, r7c4, r8c2, r8c4 on {19} (type 1): if r8c4 were 1 or 9, the four cells could swap 1 and 9 and the puzzle would have two solutions. So 1 and 9 can be removed from r8c4.

steps.text: Look at the four cells r7c2, r7c4, r8c2 and r8c4. They form a rectangle that spans exactly two boxes, and all four contain *1* and *9*.
If all four ended up as just 1/9, you could swap the 1s and 9s and get a second solution — a "deadly pattern". This puzzle has exactly one solution, so that cannot happen.
r7c2, r7c4 and r8c2 hold only 1 and 9. So the fourth corner *r8c4* must be something else — it is the only thing that can break the pattern.
So remove *1* and *9* from r8c4.

example.task: Find the unique rectangle and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

step.name: Unique Rectangle
step.text: Unique rectangle r2c7, r2c9, r5c7, r5c9 on {23} (type 1): if r5c7 were 2 or 3, the four cells could swap 2 and 3 and the puzzle would have two solutions. So 2 and 3 can be removed from r5c7.

steps.text: Look at the four cells r2c7, r2c9, r5c7 and r5c9. They form a rectangle that spans exactly two boxes, and all four contain *2* and *3*.
If all four ended up as just 2/3, you could swap the 2s and 3s and get a second solution — a "deadly pattern". This puzzle has exactly one solution, so that cannot happen.
r2c7, r2c9 and r5c9 hold only 2 and 3. So the fourth corner *r5c7* must be something else — it is the only thing that can break the pattern.
So remove *2* and *3* from r5c7.

practice.task: Find the unique rectangle and tap every candidate it removes, then press Check.

lessons.title: BUG+1
lessons.summary: All cells bivalue except one: that one is decided.
intro: A *BUG* (Bivalue Universal Grave) is a state where every empty cell has exactly two candidates and every digit appears exactly twice in each unit. Such a grid can never have a unique solution.
In *BUG+1*, all cells are bivalue except one cell with three candidates. To avoid the deadly BUG, that cell must take the candidate that would otherwise appear *three* times in its units.
How to spot it: late in a hard puzzle, when nearly every note has two digits, find the lone three-candidate cell and place the digit that is "too many" in its row, column and box.

step.name: BUG+1
step.text: BUG+1: every unsolved cell has two candidates except r1c3. Without 8 there, the grid would be a deadly pattern with two solutions, so r1c3 must be 8.

steps.text: Every unsolved cell has exactly two candidates — except *r1c3*, which has three: {4,8,9}.
If r1c3 were 4 or 9, every cell would be bivalue with each digit twice per unit: a "BUG", which can never have a unique solution.
In its row, column and box, 8 appears three times — one too many for a BUG. So *r1c3 must be 8*.

example.task: Every cell but one has two candidates. Tap the digit that must go in the odd cell.

step.name: BUG+1
step.text: BUG+1: every unsolved cell has two candidates except r2c5. Without 2 there, the grid would be a deadly pattern with two solutions, so r2c5 must be 2.

steps.text: Every unsolved cell has exactly two candidates — except *r2c5*, which has three: {2,3,7}.
If r2c5 were 3 or 7, every cell would be bivalue with each digit twice per unit: a "BUG", which can never have a unique solution.
In its row, column and box, 2 appears three times — one too many for a BUG. So *r2c5 must be 2*.

practice.task: Every cell but one has two candidates. Tap the digit that must go in the odd cell.

lessons.title: X-Chain
lessons.summary: A single-digit chain of strong and weak links.
intro: An *X-Chain* follows one digit through alternating *strong links* (a unit with only two places: if one is false, the other is true) and *weak links* (two cells that see each other: if one is true, the other is false).
Start by assuming the first cell is *not* the digit, and follow the links: false → true → false → … → true at the end. So either the first cell or the last cell holds the digit.
Any cell that sees *both ends* of the chain cannot hold the digit. Skyscrapers and kites are just short X-Chains.

step.name: X-Chain
step.text: X-Chain on 4: (4)r1c4 = (4)r1c3 - (4)r3c1 = (4)r9c1 - (4)r9c5 = (4)r5c5. Either (4)r1c4 or (4)r5c5 is true, so 4 can be removed from r5c4.

steps.text: Look only at digit *4*. Start the chain at r1c4: *suppose r1c4 is not 4* (shown in orange: "false").

Follow the links. Solid lines are strong links (if one end is false, the other is true); dashed lines are weak links (if one end is true, the other is false). If r1c4 is not 4, then *r1c3 is 4* (4 has only two places in row 1), so *r3c1 is not 4* (they share box 1), then *r9c1 is 4* (4 has only two places in column 1), so *r9c5 is not 4* (they share row 9), then *r5c5 is 4* (4 has only two places in column 5).
So if the start is not 4, the end is. *Either r1c4 or r5c5 is 4*, and any cell that sees both cannot be 4: remove *4* from r5c4.

steps.text: Look only at digit *6*. Start the chain at r2c9: *suppose r2c9 is not 6* (shown in orange: "false").

lessons.title: XY-Chain
lessons.summary: A chain through two-candidate cells.
intro: An *XY-Chain* hops through cells with exactly *two candidates*. Inside a cell the link is strong (if it is not one digit, it is the other); between cells that see each other it is weak (they cannot share a digit).
Assume the first cell is *not* Z. Then it is its other digit, which forces the next cell, and so on, until the last cell is forced to be *Z*. So either the start or the end is Z.
Cells that see both ends lose Z. An XY-Wing is simply an XY-Chain of three cells.

step.name: XY-Chain
step.text: XY-Chain: (8)r1c1 = (5)r1c1 - (5)r1c9 = (1)r1c9 - (1)r6c9 = (3)r6c9 - (3)r6c3 = (8)r6c3. Either (8)r1c1 or (8)r6c3 is true, so 8 can be removed from r2c3, r4c1.

steps.text: Look at the cells with exactly two candidates. Start the chain at r1c1: *suppose r1c1 is not 8* (shown in orange: "false").

Follow the links. Solid lines are strong links (if one end is false, the other is true); dashed lines are weak links (if one end is true, the other is false). If r1c1 is not 8, then *r1c1 is 5* (r1c1 holds only 8 and 5), so *r1c9 is not 5* (they share row 1), then *r1c9 is 1* (r1c9 holds only 5 and 1), so *r6c9 is not 1* (they share column 9).
Keep going: then *r6c9 is 3* (r6c9 holds only 1 and 3), so *r6c3 is not 3* (they share row 6), then *r6c3 is 8* (r6c3 holds only 3 and 8). Teal means "true", orange "false".
So if the start is not 8, the end is. *Either r1c1 or r6c3 is 8*, and any cell that sees both cannot be 8: remove *8* from r2c3 and r4c1.

step.name: XY-Chain
step.text: XY-Chain: (1)r3c4 = (9)r3c4 - (9)r3c5 = (7)r3c5 - (7)r6c5 = (2)r6c5 - (2)r6c2 = (1)r6c2. Either (1)r3c4 or (1)r6c2 is true, so 1 can be removed from r6c4.

steps.text: Look at the cells with exactly two candidates. Start the chain at r3c4: *suppose r3c4 is not 1* (shown in orange: "false").

Follow the links. Solid lines are strong links (if one end is false, the other is true); dashed lines are weak links (if one end is true, the other is false). If r3c4 is not 1, then *r3c4 is 9* (r3c4 holds only 1 and 9), so *r3c5 is not 9* (they share row 3), then *r3c5 is 7* (r3c5 holds only 9 and 7), so *r6c5 is not 7* (they share column 5).
Keep going: then *r6c5 is 2* (r6c5 holds only 7 and 2), so *r6c2 is not 2* (they share row 6), then *r6c2 is 1* (r6c2 holds only 2 and 1). Teal means "true", orange "false".
So if the start is not 1, the end is. *Either r3c4 or r6c2 is 1*, and any cell that sees both cannot be 1: remove *1* from r6c4.

lessons.title: WXYZ-Wing
lessons.summary: Four cells, four digits, one non-restricted digit.
intro: A *WXYZ-Wing* is four cells, all within reach of a pivot, whose candidates use only *four digits* together.

For three of the digits, all cells holding them see each other, so each can be used at most once. That covers at most three of the four cells — the fourth must be *Z*, the one digit whose cells do not all see each other.
So one of the Z cells is Z, and any cell that sees *all* of them loses Z. It is the XYZ-Wing idea grown by one cell.

step.name: WXYZ-Wing
step.text: WXYZ-Wing: the four cells r6c4, r4c4, r6c2, r8c4 hold only the digits 1, 5, 8 and 9. Every digit except 9 can appear at most once among them, so at least one of r4c4, r6c2 must be 9: 9 can be removed from r4c2.

steps.text: Look at the four cells r6c4, r4c4, r6c2 and r8c4: r6c4 {1,8}, r4c4 {5,9}, r6c2 {1,9}, r8c4 {5,8}. Together they use only *1, 5, 8 and 9*.
For every digit except 9, the cells holding it all see each other, so each of those digits can be used at most once here. Three digits can fill at most three of the four cells.
So the remaining cell must be *9*: at least one of r4c4 and r6c2 is 9.
Any cell that sees all of them can't be 9: remove *9* from r4c2.

step.name: WXYZ-Wing
step.text: WXYZ-Wing: the four cells r8c5, r2c5, r6c5, r9c4 hold only the digits 5, 6, 7 and 9. Every digit except 5 can appear at most once among them, so at least one of r6c5, r9c4 must be 5: 5 can be removed from r7c5.

steps.text: Look at the four cells r8c5, r2c5, r6c5 and r9c4: r8c5 {6,7}, r2c5 {7,9}, r6c5 {5,9}, r9c4 {5,6}. Together they use only *5, 6, 7 and 9*.
For every digit except 5, the cells holding it all see each other, so each of those digits can be used at most once here. Three digits can fill at most three of the four cells.
So the remaining cell must be *5*: at least one of r6c5 and r9c4 is 5.
Any cell that sees all of them can't be 5: remove *5* from r7c5.

lessons.title: Alternating Inference Chain
lessons.summary: Chains that mix digits and cells freely.
intro: An *alternating inference chain* (AIC) combines everything: strong links inside units and inside two-candidate cells, weak links between peers and between digits of one cell.
The rule never changes: assume the start is false, and follow strong (false → true) and weak (true → false) links alternately. You end on something true, so *the start or the end must be true*.

What that removes depends on the ends: the same digit in two cells clears common peers; two digits in one cell clear the cell's other candidates; different digits in cells that see each other remove one from the other.

step.name: Alternating Inference Chain
step.text: Alternating inference chain: (5)r1c7 = (5)r7c7 - (5)r7c2 = (7)r7c2 - (7)r7c9 = (7)r1c9. Either (5)r1c7 or (7)r1c9 is true, so 7 can be removed from r1c7.

steps.text: Chains can mix digits and cells. Start the chain at r1c7: *suppose r1c7 is not 5* (shown in orange: "false").

Follow the links. Solid lines are strong links (if one end is false, the other is true); dashed lines are weak links (if one end is true, the other is false). If r1c7 is not 5, then *r7c7 is 5* (5 has only two places in column 7), so *r7c2 is not 5* (they share row 7), then *r7c2 is 7* (r7c2 holds only 5 and 7), so *r7c9 is not 7* (they share row 7), then *r1c9 is 7* (7 has only two places in column 9).

So *r1c7 is 5 or r1c9 is 7* (at least one). The two cells see each other: if r1c7 were 7, it would not be 5, and r1c9 could not be 7 either — both ends false, which is impossible. Remove *7* from r1c7.

step.name: Alternating Inference Chain
step.text: Alternating inference chain: (7)r1c9 = (7)r4c9 - (7)r4c5 = (2)r4c5 - (2)r5c5 = (2)r5c9. Either (7)r1c9 or (2)r5c9 is true, so 2 can be removed from r1c9.

steps.text: Chains can mix digits and cells. Start the chain at r1c9: *suppose r1c9 is not 7* (shown in orange: "false").

Follow the links. Solid lines are strong links (if one end is false, the other is true); dashed lines are weak links (if one end is true, the other is false). If r1c9 is not 7, then *r4c9 is 7* (7 has only two places in column 9), so *r4c5 is not 7* (they share row 4), then *r4c5 is 2* (r4c5 holds only 7 and 2), so *r5c5 is not 2* (they share column 5), then *r5c9 is 2* (2 has only two places in row 5).

So *r1c9 is 7 or r5c9 is 2* (at least one). The two cells see each other: if r1c9 were 2, it would not be 7, and r5c9 could not be 2 either — both ends false, which is impossible. Remove *2* from r1c9.

lessons.title: Forcing Chain
lessons.summary: Try every option; whatever they agree on is true.
intro: A *forcing chain* is the last resort before guessing — and it is still pure logic. Take a cell with few candidates (or a digit with few places in a unit) and try *each option in turn*, following only the obvious forced moves.

If one option leads to a contradiction (a cell with no candidates, or a unit with no place for a digit), that option is false. If *every* option leads to the same placement or removal, that result is true no matter what.
Forcing chains are powerful but long. Use them when nothing else works, and keep the branches short.

step.name: Forcing Chain
step.text: Forcing chain: if r1c3 were 5, following the forced moves r5c8 would be left without a valid digit. So 5 can be removed from r1c3.

steps.text: Nothing simpler works here, so we test an option. Suppose *r1c3 is 5*.
Follow only the forced moves (singles): r2c3 = 4, r1c9 = 4, r1c5 = 6, r2c5 = 7 and 13 more. The shaded cells show this imagined line of play.
Now *r5c8 is left with no candidate at all (and so is r4c3)* — a contradiction. The assumption "r1c3 is 5" must be false.
Back on the real board: remove *5* from r1c3.

example.task: Suppose r1c3 were 5, and follow the forced singles. Is that possible? Tap the candidate you can remove, then press Check.

step.name: Forcing Chain
step.text: Forcing chain: if r1c7 were 4, following the forced moves box 9 would have no place for 7. So 4 can be removed from r1c7.

steps.text: Nothing simpler works here, so we test an option. Suppose *r1c7 is 4*.
Follow only the forced moves (singles): r1c8 = 5, r7c1 = 5, r8c9 = 4, r8c7 = 5 and 9 more. The shaded cells show this imagined line of play.
Now *box 9 has no place left for 7* — a contradiction. The assumption "r1c7 is 4" must be false.
Back on the real board: remove *4* from r1c7.
